content: Participants were deemed eligible for two birth cohort studies. In the current analysis, all participants from the 1982 birth cohort and young adults from a subsample of the 1993 cohort, who had complete data on breastfeeding during the first four years of life, were included. The subsample from the 1993 cohort consisted of all low birth weight children (less than 2500 grams) and a random sample of 20% of the remaining original cohort. Breastfeeding information was collected prospectively during the first four years of life through home interviews with mothers. In a study conducted in Mbeya city, Tanzania, a quota sampling technique was used to select children aged 2–4 years based on rural-urban strata and age distribution from the 2012 census. Mothers and children were asked to assemble at designated locations for interviews and examinations. Mothers or caregivers were interviewed about demographic characteristics, breastfeeding, and weaning practices. Breastfeeding duration was recorded as 1 year, more than 1 year up to 2 years, or more than 2 years. This was dichotomized into 1 year and more than 1 year, coded as 0 and 1, respectively. A cross-sectional study in Lusaka, Zambia, surveyed randomly selected clusters of households. Mothers (93% of interviews) or close relatives provided information on breastfeeding duration, defined as the age at which breastfeeding completely ceased. Data from the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (KNHANES) from 2010 to 2013 were analyzed. Of the 25,712 participants, exclusions included males, individuals under 30 years, nulliparous individuals, those with missing data, and those diagnosed with diabetes before their first delivery. Data from 9,960 parous women were analyzed. Participants were asked about their breastfeeding history, total breastfeeding duration, and the number of children breastfed. Average breastfeeding duration per child was calculated by dividing the total breastfeeding duration by the number of children breastfed. Participants were categorized into groups based on total breastfeeding duration (none, 1–12 months, 13–24 months, 25–36 months, and over 36 months) and average breastfeeding duration per child (none, 1–6 months, 7–12 months, 13–18 months, and over 18 months). The Healthy Kids Queensland Physical Activity and Nutrition Survey (2006) provided data on early feeding behaviors and anthropometry. Parents were asked direct questions about breastfeeding, including whether the child was ever breastfed, the duration of exclusive breastfeeding, and the age at which the child started eating solid foods. The Andhra Pradesh Children and Parents Study (APCAPS) provided retrospective breastfeeding data from mothers during a 2003–2005 follow-up survey when children were aged 13–18 years. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups: up to 12 months, more than 12 but less than 24 months, more than 24 but less than 36 months, and over 36 months. The India Human Development Surveys (IHDS) of 2004–2005 and 2011–2012 collected breastfeeding data for the two youngest children born to each mother. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups: up to 6 months, more than 6 but less than 12 months, more than 12 but less than 24 months, and over 24 months. The Nord-Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT) in Norway targeted adults over 19 years of age. Exclusion criteria included non-response to the second questionnaire, current pregnancy, age over 85 years, non-attendance at clinical examinations, self-reported cardiovascular conditions or diabetes before the first live birth, less than one year since the last childbirth, unknown lactation history, and use of antihypertensive medication. Lifetime lactation duration was calculated as the sum of lactation durations for all live births and categorized into five levels (none, 1–6 months, 7–12 months, 13–23 months, and 24 months or more). Outcomes included body mass index, waist circumference, triglycerides, HDL, LDL, cholesterol, hypertension, and obesity. The Pelotas Birth Cohort in Brazil followed children born in 1993. In 2004–2005, all cohort participants, except those known to have died, were eligible for follow-up. Breastfeeding exposures included total breastfeeding duration, predominant breastfeeding duration (breast milk with water, teas, or juice but no solid or semi-solid foods), ever breastfed, and introduction of solid or semi-solid foods before four months of age. Outcomes included overweight and obesity, defined using BMI and skinfold measurements. The 45 and Up Study in New South Wales, Australia, included women aged 45 years and older who completed a baseline questionnaire. Exclusion criteria included a history of cardiovascular disease, nulliparity, or unknown parity. Breastfeeding duration per child was categorized as never breastfed, less than 6 months, 6–12 months, or more than 12 months. The Prospective Cohort Study of Thai Children (PCTC) in Thailand recruited pregnant women at 23–38 weeks of gestation and followed their children until 24 years of age. Due to funding and administrative issues, the project ended in 2005. Breastfeeding was categorized as exclusive breastfeeding (only breast milk, no water or other liquids), full breastfeeding (breast milk with or without water or other liquids but no formula), and any breastfeeding (breast milk with or without formula or foods). Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four groups: less than 6 months, 6–11 months, 12–17 months, and 18 months or more. A cross-sectional study in Viçosa, Brazil, included children aged 6–10 years enrolled in public and private schools. A questionnaire was administered to mothers to assess family characteristics, maternal conditions during pregnancy, the child’s birth, breastfeeding duration, and physical activity practices. The 2010 Rwanda Demographic and Health Survey collected data from 492 randomly selected villages, with 26 households per village. Data on children aged 2 years or younger were used to assess stunting prevalence. Predictors included early initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding under 6 months, continued breastfeeding at 1 year, and introduction of solid, semi-solid, or soft foods. A retrospective cohort study in São Luís, Brazil, examined preschool children from low-income populations. Breastfeeding beyond 1 year and early childhood caries (ECC) were common in this population. Children were selected from four community daycare centers in peripheral neighborhoods.
